performers: Royal Albert Hall Orchestra, Edward Elgar
recorded: 27 April 1926, Queen’s Hall, London; issued by Victor in 1927
intro: Elgar conducts the Royal Albert Hall Orchestra in his first electrical recording of the march, made in 1926. The famous trio sits inside a quick march marked “with much fire”.

sections.label: Intro · An off-beat shout
sections.mNote: The orchestra starts in E♭, a semitone above home

sections.label: A · The quick march
sections.mNote: Short string phrases over a bounding bass

sections.label: B · The trio in G major
sections.mNote: Violins, clarinets and horns share the long tune

sections.label: A′ · The quick march returns
sections.mNote: The strings recover their short, accented phrases

sections.label: B′ · The trio in D major
sections.mNote: The broad tune returns, marked Molto maestoso

sections.label: Coda · One last burst of marching
sections.mNote: Quick figures interrupt the broad tune

cues.title: A start in E♭
cues.text: Elgar begins his D-major march with an off-beat shout in E♭. The orchestra has to find its way down a semitone before the march can settle into its stride. Above the first bar he writes Allegro, con molto fuoco: fast, with much fire.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, opening page and rehearsal A. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/6e/IMSLP24159-PMLP23738-Elgar_-_Pomp_and_Circumstance%2C_Op._39%2C_No._1.pdf. The opening E♭ is also discussed by the Elgar Society: https://www.elgar.org/3pomp.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Elgar’s first recording, cut to four minutes
cues.text: Elgar’s first recording of this march, on 26 June 1914, is cut to just over four minutes. It begins with the trio tune so that none of the trio is lost, and some thirty London players make the orchestra. The 1926 recording heard here is his first complete one.
cues.evidence: Elgar Society, “Pomp and Circumstance: Elgar’s own recordings”: the acoustic session of 26 June 1914 and the first complete recording on 27 April 1926 at Queen’s Hall. https://www.elgar.org/3pomp-d.htm

cues.title: The tune before the words
cues.text: The trio opens in G major, marked Largamente. First violins, clarinets and horns share a long melody over a steady accompaniment. This is the tune that becomes Land of Hope and Glory; here it begins quietly, without a singer or a crowd.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal I, Trio, p. 138 in the linked reprint. The later setting of the tune is documented at https://www.elgar.org/3pomp.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: As though it were new
cues.text: In November 1931, opening the Abbey Road studios, Elgar addresses the London Symphony Orchestra before conducting this tune: “Please play this tune as though you’ve never heard it before.” Pathé’s cameras preserve the request.
cues.evidence: Elgar to the London Symphony Orchestra, Abbey Road, 12 November 1931, filmed by Pathé. The words and occasion are transcribed by the Elgar Society: https://www.elgar.org/3pomp-d.htm

cues.title: The march gets moving
cues.text: A tempo: the strings recover their short, accented phrases in D major. Running notes flicker between the heavier beats, and the bass resumes its bounding figure. The broad trio has left plenty of marching still to do.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal M, p. 143 in the linked reprint: return of the march, a tempo, with the D-major key signature restored.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: D major, much broader
cues.text: The trio returns in D major, the march’s home key. Elgar marks it Molto maestoso. The melody now climbs high above the bass, with the full orchestra supporting the long notes that first sounded so quietly.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, after rehearsal R, Molto maestoso, pp. 150–153 in the linked reprint.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The march has the last word
cues.text: The long tune releases its hold. Quick string figures return, woodwinds pass short notes down through the orchestra, and Elgar closes with a sharp chord followed by a final held D.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal T to the end, pp. 153–154 in the linked reprint: a tempo, then Più mosso and the final cadence.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Royal Albert Hall Orchestra (orchestra), Edward Elgar (conductor)
fields.note: The label explicitly says conducted by Sir Edward Elgar; the composer credit alone was not used to infer this role.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The Elgar Society identifies this as Elgar’s first complete recording of the march, distinguishing it from the severely cut 1914 acoustic version. Complete does not establish that every written repeat was taken. The precise performing edition and organ participation are not established.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Independently documented in the Elgar Society recording account and Naxos 8.111022 discography. Internet Archive’s date 1927 concerns the Victor issue, not the recording session. The identifier retains that issue year.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue is printed on the disc label; it is not inferred from the orchestra’s Royal Albert Hall name.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The label says Orthophonic Recording, identifying the electrical process.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Victor 9016 couples Marches Nos. 1 and 2; the January 1927 trade listing identifies the same performers.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The specialist Naxos discography lists matrix CR 336-2 and original British issue HMV D 1102. The transferred pressing’s take suffix is not independently legible. Internet Archive’s matrix 9016A is the issue-side number, and its other ID CR331 is not silently adopted as the master number.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: George Blood, L.P.; Phoebe Pugh, transfer
fields.note: The item identifies the digitisation facility and user_transferred field; these are transfer credits, not original session personnel.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The November 2023 upload does not establish the transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Digitised at 78 rpm; preferred 3.8 mil truncated-conical stylus transfer; equalised with turnover 250 and rolloff 0; MP3 derivative
fields.note: The original FLAC’s embedded comment identifies the selected stylus and equalisation. The site uses the supplied preferred MP3 without joining or changing the audio.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Elgar’s original 1901 march is public domain in ordinary life-plus-70 jurisdictions
fields.note: Elgar died in 1934. This concerns the underlying composition, not an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: Victor 9016 announced for publication on 28 January 1927
fields.note: Rule 3. The Talking Machine World, 15 January 1927, p. 131, lists 9016 under the Victor list for 28 January, naming both marches and Elgar with the Royal Albert Hall Orchestra. This is publication evidence, not a session-date substitution; the British first issue may be earlier. Its 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established. The selected Great 78 item, original FLAC and label were checked; no NC licence or separate upstream digital recording is stated. The Naxos booklet is used only as documentary evidence: its commercial restoration is not the selected audio.

composer.epithet: He made the Enigma Variations from his friendships and preserved his own way with the music on gramophone records.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. His education continued in rehearsal rooms. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn from inside the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. Here was an orchestra whose players he knew individually, with capabilities he had to accommodate. His other work included teaching in local schools and giving private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
